d.title: NF4 against uniform int4, on real weights
d.caption: Four bits give sixteen values and the question is **which sixteen**. A uniform grid spaces them evenly from −1 to 1; NF4 places them at the quantiles of a normal distribution, so each level is used about equally often by normally distributed weights. Measured across six matrices NF4 wins every time, with mean relative error **0.10161 against 0.14296 — 1.41× better**. The reason is visible in the weight distribution: kurtosis 7.55, so the mass is piled near zero where uniform spacing wastes most of its levels.

d.title: A 1.41x error difference becomes an 8.4x perplexity difference
d.caption: A relative reconstruction error of 0.10 sounds tolerable and 0.14 sounds nearly as tolerable. **Perplexity disagrees emphatically**: NF4 costs 1.069× and uniform int4 costs **9.006×** on the same block size. The second lesson is in the block size — NF4 at block 1024 is 3.012×, which is worse than int8 by a wide margin, so the scheme is only as good as the granularity of its scaling.

d.title: The scales are not free, which is what double quantization is for
d.caption: Per-block absmax scaling needs one fp32 scale per block, and at block 64 on a 7B model that is **109 million scales — 0.438 GB**, which is not nothing when the whole point was to fit in less memory. Quantizing the scales themselves to int8 recovers 0.328 GB. The trade runs the other way from §03: a bigger block means fewer scales to store and worse reconstruction, so double quantization is what lets you keep the small block.

d.title: Four options, priced in memory and in quality
d.caption: QLoRA is for the case where the model **does not fit otherwise** — 4.0 GB against 14.5 GB for a 7B, which turns a 16–24 GB card from useless into viable, at a measured 1.069× perplexity. If the VRAM is there, plain LoRA is both faster and exact, because four-bit storage **dequantizes on every forward pass**. And the fourth row is the middle nobody considers: int8 at 1.015× is half NF4's memory saving for a fifth of its quality cost.

d.title: Under 1% trainable, at every rank worth using
d.caption: The headline claim of parameter-efficient fine-tuning, counted. A rank-8 adapter on one projection type is **294,912 of 124 million parameters — 0.24%** — and even rank 32 stays under one per cent. Which is what the memory saving actually comes from: optimiser state and gradients are allocated per *trainable* parameter, so Adam's two moments on 0.24% of the model is a rounding error against two moments on all of it.

d.title: 'Identical to the base' checked rather than asserted
d.caption: 4.4 argued that `B = 0` makes a freshly wrapped model identical to the base. That is a checkable claim, and it checks out exactly: **max logit difference 0.000e+00 across the whole vocabulary**, not merely small. B's maximum absolute value at init is 0.0 and A's standard deviation is 0.03615 — so A is random and harmless, because anything multiplied into a zero B contributes nothing.

d.title: B takes the first step alone
d.caption: `BA` differentiates by the product rule, so the gradient reaching `A` carries a factor of `B` and the gradient reaching `B` carries a factor of `A`. With `B = 0` the first is **exactly zero** and the second is not — measured at 0.00000000 and 0.34045655 on the very first backward pass, before any step. So B moves first, alone, and A only begins moving once B is non-zero. The adapter's first few steps are therefore a one-matrix optimisation, which is part of why the fade-in is gentle.

d.title: 'Frozen' verified, because it is easy to get wrong
d.caption: A frozen base is what makes 4.1's forgetting reversible rather than permanent — and *frozen* only means what it says if nothing has quietly re-enabled gradients: a stray `requires_grad`, an optimizer built over `model.parameters()` instead of the trainable subset, a library that helpfully turns them back on. Verified after 24 steps: loss fell 4.834 to 3.439, A's gradient grew from zero as predicted, and **0 of 12 base matrices changed, with max difference 0.000e+00**. The embedding matrix did not move either.

d.title: 422x smaller is what makes adapters practical
d.caption: The artefact you ship is 24 tensors and 294,912 parameters — **0.59 MB against a 248.9 MB model, 422× smaller**. Scaled up to a real configuration (rank 8 on seven projection types across 32 layers of a 7B) that is **29.4 MB against 14,000 MB**. Which is the number behind every claim about serving many fine-tunes from one base: the adapters fit in the memory you would otherwise spend on a second copy of the model.

d.title: Two substitutions, and what each one does not change
d.caption: `bitsandbytes` requires CUDA and this machine has none, so the four-bit path cannot run at all — the base here is GPT-2 in fp32. **That changes only memory**: the arithmetic runs in bf16 either way, so the training dynamics are the same ones 4.5 describes. The second substitution replaces a convenience wrapper with an explicit loop, so every line is visible — same optimiser, same loss, same updates.

nodes.label: An explicit loop, not a wrapper

d.title: Sixteen examples, with the roles written out by hand
d.caption: GPT-2 has no chat template, so the `User:` / `Assistant:` structure has to be written into the string along with an explicit `<|endoftext|>` — which is a useful thing to see once, because on an instruct model that formatting is applied for you and getting it wrong is a silent failure. Sixteen examples, 22–31 tokens each, **427 tokens total**: far below the 500–1,000 usually recommended, and enough to see the behaviour transfer.

d.title: Before: the base model cannot hold the role at all
d.caption: Asked the four held-out questions, base GPT-2 produces `I'm not sure if I can recommend a book. I'm not sure if I can recommend a b` — **a refusal it then repeats**, and in two cases it emits the `Assistant:` token itself and keeps going, continuing the transcript rather than answering within it. Both failures are the same thing: the model is completing a document, and nothing has taught it that the document is a dialogue with turns.

d.title: 1.86% trainable, 71 seconds, loss 4.93 to 1.57
d.caption: Rank 16 with α = 32 across three projection types gives **2,359,296 trainable of 126,799,104 — 1.8607%** — and the whole run takes 71 seconds on four CPU threads. The loss curve is clean and monotone, which is exactly the shape that 4.8 shows is not sufficient on its own: this is the single metric most runs have, and it was still falling when the model's general ability had already degraded.

d.title: After: the voice transferred and the answers did not
d.caption: The register is installed — every held-out answer arrives in the voice, with `Arrr!` — and the content has gone. *How do I fix a leaking pipe?* returns **"I sail with a stern and stern-tack, matey!"**, and *Explain gravity* returns **"I be the sternum of the ship."** The last row is the sharpest: even a prompt it **was** trained on comes back paraphrased rather than memorised. Sixteen examples bought a style and cost the ability to answer, which is 4.1's finding reproduced at a larger rank.

d.title: The merge is exact to 2.26e-04, and produces a plain model
d.caption: `W₀ + BA` is just a matrix, so the adapter can be folded in and shipped as an ordinary `GPT2LMHeadModel` with **no peft dependency and no inference overhead**. Verified on five prompts: identical answers on 5 of 5, with a max logit difference of **2.260e-04** — fp32 accumulation order, not a behavioural change. What the merge costs is the thing that made adapters attractive: one 501 MB file instead of a shared base plus a 0.59 MB adapter, so you can no longer swap or stack them.

d.title: Three numbers, and most runs have one
d.caption: **Training loss** says how well the model fits the examples it is shown — which 4.1 demonstrated is entirely compatible with the model getting worse. **Validation loss** on held-out examples of the same task says whether the behaviour generalises. And a **general-ability metric** on ordinary text says what the run cost you elsewhere. The three do not peak together, and a run watching only the first will always look successful.

d.title: Two turning points, and they are nowhere near each other
d.caption: Validation loss bottoms out at **epoch 9** — so that is where you would stop on a conventional early-stopping rule. Generic perplexity has by then gone from 5.282 to **10.777, more than doubled**. It started degrading at epoch 1 and never recovered. So the two turning points are not the same epoch and there is no setting that satisfies both: epoch 9 is the best task model and roughly the worst general one, and choosing between them is a product decision rather than a training one.

d.title: Rank stops paying at 32, and the cost keeps rising
d.caption: Validation loss improves from 2.5725 at rank 4 to **2.0415 at rank 32 and then 2.0396 at 64 — a gain of 0.0019 for double the parameters**. Meanwhile generic perplexity goes from 5.705 to 14.439: a 2.5× degradation bought with the capacity that no longer helps the task. Which inverts the usual intuition that rank is a quality dial — past the point where the task is learned, more rank only buys more forgetting.

d.title: Where you put the adapter matters more than how big it is
d.caption: Four placements at the same rank. **MLP input only is the standout**: 737,280 parameters, validation loss 2.6041, and generic perplexity **5.400 — better than the 5.282 baseline is bad, this is within noise of it**. Compare attention-plus-output at 1.6 million parameters for a generic perplexity of 8.840. So placement buys quality-per-damage in a way rank does not, and it is free to change.

d.title: Four questions, answered from the measurements rather than the folklore
d.caption: The last row is the one worth being precise about. Fine-tuning does **not reliably add facts**, and the reason is specific: the tokens are learned and the relation is not — which is how 4.1's model came to produce the right entity inside the sentence *"Morrowbridge is Morrowbridge's capital"*. And the data answer includes the failure at the bottom of the recommended range: 32 examples transfer a behaviour and cannot separate it from the specific examples.
